tutorial.title: Shopping List App
tutorial.descriptionContent: Create a program to help Rachel get all the items she needs when going shopping

executableContent.instructions:
Rachel often forgets to purchase some things when she goes to the grocery store. Develop an app to help her manage a shopping list!

Rachel plans to go to the supermarket tomorrow. She checks the house and writes down a list of items she needs. Let's create a variable to represent the shopping list.

1. Create a `shopping_list` variable and set `["potato", "apple", "oil", "milk", "toilet paper"]` as its value.

Rachel's dad wants her to buy some batteries for him. Let's append a new `batteries` item to the shopping list.

1. Call the `append()` function on `shopping_list` to append `"batteries"` to the shopping list.
2. Print `shopping_list` to confirm that the shopping list includes the batteries.

hints.title: Hint
hints.content: Remember that the syntax to append a value into a list is: `list.append(value)`

executableContent.instructions:
Rachel's sister, Riley, loves chocolate and Rachel knows a store in the supermarket where they sell fair-trade and really good quality chocolate. Since the store is at the entrance of the supermarket, let's make it the first item on the list to spare Rachel the detour!

1. Before the print statement, call the `insert()` function on `shopping_list` to insert `"chocolate"` as the first item of the shopping list. We can confirm that chocolate is on the shopping list when it is printed.

hints.title: Hint
hints.content: Remember that `insert()` takes 2 parameters, the index to insert the value, and the value itself. The syntax to insert an element into a list is: `list.insert(index, value)`

executableContent.instructions:
Rachel just remembered that Riley only likes dark chocolate. We already inserted `"chocolate"` into the list but we can change it to `"dark chocolate"`.

1. Before the print statement, change the value of the first element of the `shopping_list` from `"chocolate"` to `"dark chocolate"`, using its list index. We can confirm the change when the list is printed.

files.name: script.py
files.solvedContent:
shopping_list = ["potato", "apple", "oil", "milk","toilet paper"]
shopping_list.append("batteries")
shopping_list.insert(0, "chocolate")
shopping_list[0] = "dark chocolate"
print(shopping_list)

hints.title: Hint
hints.content: Remember you can change the value of an element in a list when you access it. The syntax is as follows: `list[index] = new value`

executableContent.instructions:
Rachel's dad just called to inform Rachel that he found some batteries in the garage. Let's take the `batteries` out of the shopping list.

1. Before the print statement, call the `pop()` function on `shopping_list` to take `"batteries"` out of the shopping list. We can confirm that batteries are out of the shopping list when it is printed.

hints.title: Hint
hints.content: Remember that the syntax to pop an element out of a list is: `list.pop(index)` if index is not specified, the default value is `-1`, which is the last item.

1. Create a `purchased_list` variable and set `["dark chocolate", "potato", "apple", "oil", "toilet paper", "fish fingers"]` as its value.
2. Create a `unavailable_items` variable and set `[]` as its value.

executableContent.instructions:
Rachel wants to make sure that she's bought everything that was on the shopping list. Let's go through the shopping list and see if each item is on the purchased list as well. If it is not on the purchased list, we'll add it to the list of items that she did not purchase.

1. Loop through `shopping_list` using a for-loop.
2. For every item in `shopping_list`, check if the item is **not** in `purchased_list`.
3. If the above condition is fulfilled, append the item to `unavailable_items`.

print(shopping_list)

purchased_list = ["dark chocolate", "potato", "apple", "oil", "toilet paper", "fish fingers"]

unavailable_items = []
for item in shopping_list:
  if item not in purchased_list:
    unavailable_items.append(item)

executableContent.instructions:
Awesome! We have the items she didn't manage to buy. Let's print them so that Rachel can see what she needs to buy next time. If there are no items on the list, we'll print a message to let her know that she managed to purchase everything she needed.

1. After the for-loop, check if the length of `unavailable_items` is greater than `0`.
2. If the condition mentioned above is fulfilled, print this f-string:
`f"Here's a list of items on your shopping list that you did not purchase: {unavailable_items}"`
3. Code an `else` block after the `if` block. 
4. Print the following f-string within the `else` block:
```
f"Good job! You bought everything on your shopping list!"
```
